risks: The protocol is already approved practice; the main risk is harm during interruption (self-extubation, agitation), which is monitored and reviewed at every huddle, and blame on individual nurses, which is avoided by reporting unit-level data only.
consent: No individual consent: the redesign supports an approved protocol; families are given a short explanation of morning awakening, with an interpreter when needed.
data: The tally sheet holds bed number, date and completion only; unit-level weekly data are posted; no patient identifiers leave the unit.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families who do not speak the unit's main language may not understand why their relative is woken, and patients with limited English may be judged agitated when they are frightened. Interpreter access is part of the morning routine and missed interruptions attributed to agitation are reviewed for these patients.
effectiveness: Success means a sustained shift in completed interruptions with no rise in self-extubation or rescue boluses.
efficiency: About five minutes a day of charge nurse time and the facilitator's four hours a week.
partnerships: Bedside nurses, respiratory therapists, the ICU medical director and nurse manager as sponsors, and a family partner from the ICU family advisory group.
rebPath: Service improvement of an approved protocol; the hospital's quality office will be asked to confirm that no research ethics review is needed before any publication, following the TCPS 2 guidance on quality improvement.
limitations: One unit; before-after design with run charts; documentation may change faster than practice.
summary: Low-risk improvement of an approved protocol with safety monitoring and interpreter access.
